location.value: Japan, ruled by the shogun from Edo (Tokyo), with the emperor’s court in Kyoto.

terrain.value: Mountainous islands with limited farmland. The coastal sea-lanes linked Edo and Osaka.

climate.value: Temperate. Cold years caused famines (Kyōhō 1732, Tenmei 1782–88, Tenpō 1833–37).

resources.value: Rice, silver (exported to China), the Sado gold mine, and timber.

disasters.value: Famines, earthquakes and fires (e.g. the Great Fire of Meireki, 1657), and the eruption of Mount Asama (1783).

population.value: About 30 million by the 18th century. Not in the Wikipedia infobox.

urbanisation.value: Rapid urbanisation. Edo likely had over one million people around 1800, perhaps the world’s largest city.

disease.value: Smallpox and measles epidemics. Cholera arrived in 1822 and 1858.

migration.value: Japanese were forbidden to leave the country under sakoku (from the 1630s).

economicBase.value: A rice economy measured in koku, rapid commercialisation, and a rising merchant class.

tradeRoutes.value: Limited foreign trade: Dutch and Chinese ships at Nagasaki, Korea via Tsushima, and Ryukyu via Satsuma.

wealth.value: No GDP figure is given in the sources checked. A long period of growth and peace.

moneyAndTax.value: Tokugawa gold, silver and copper coins. Peasants paid rice taxes (about 40% on shogunal lands).

inequality.value: A strict four-class order (samurai, farmers, artisans, merchants), though merchants grew rich.

governmentType.value: A feudal military government (the bakuhan system): the shogun ruled with about 260 regional lords (daimyo), while the emperor was a ceremonial figure.

keyRulers.value: Tokugawa Ieyasu (1603–1605, founder). Iemitsu (sakoku). Tsunayoshi. Yoshimune (Kyōhō reforms). Yoshinobu (1866–1867, last).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Tokugawa family, with branch houses to supply heirs.

institutions.value: Alternate attendance (sankin-kōtai) kept daimyo under control. The Laws for the Military Houses (1615). Sakoku edicts (1630s).

stability.value: About 250 years of peace (Pax Tokugawa). The Shimabara Rebellion (1637–38). Thousands of peasant uprisings.

eliteConflict.value: Tension with powerful outer lords (Satsuma, Chōshū), who led the overthrow in 1867–68.

armyAndTech.value: Samurai armies. Firearms were restricted and military technology stagnated during the long peace.

majorWars.value: The Battle of Sekigahara (1600) and the Siege of Osaka (1614–15). The Boshin War (1868–69) ended the shogunate.

territoryChange.value: Stable. Ezo (Hokkaido) was gradually brought under control.

alliancesRivals.value: Controlled foreign contacts with the Dutch, China and Korea. Rivals: the Toyotomi clan, and later Western powers.

inventions.value: Advanced woodblock printing, and “Dutch learning” (rangaku) brought Western medicine and science.

scienceEducation.value: High literacy for the time through temple schools (terakoya). Western medicine studied through Dutch books.

openness.value: Largely closed (sakoku), with limited Dutch and Chinese contact, until Perry’s arrival (1853) forced it open.

communicationTransport.value: The Five Routes (Gokaidō) such as the Tōkaidō, with post towns; express foot messengers (hikyaku); coastal shipping.

religion.value: Buddhism (every family registered with a temple), Confucianism as official ideology, and Shinto. Christianity was banned and persecuted.

languageWriting.value: Early Modern Japanese, written in kanji and kana; high literacy for the time.

artsArchitecture.value: Kabuki and bunraku theatre, ukiyo-e prints (Hokusai, Hiroshige), haiku (Bashō), and the Genroku culture (1688–1704).

socialStructure.value: Samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants, plus outcastes. Women were subordinate in law.

sharedIdentity.value: A national culture grew through travel, print and pilgrimage. The National Learning (kokugaku) movement.

dailyLife.value: Wooden houses with tatami mats and paper screens; rice, miso soup, pickles and fish; public bathhouses.

neighbours.value: Qing China, Joseon Korea, the Ryukyu Kingdom, Ainu peoples, and the Dutch (Dejima).

ideasReligions.value: Received Western knowledge through the Dutch. Exported art that later influenced Europe (Japonisme).

colonisation.value: Not a coloniser, though Satsuma dominated the Ryukyu Kingdom from 1609. Faced pressure from Western powers after 1853 (unequal treaties).

riseSignals.value: Ieyasu’s victory at Sekigahara (1600), control of daimyo, and peace and stability.

peakPeriod.value: The Genroku era (1688–1704), with economic growth and urban culture.

declineSignals.value: Fixed rice taxes losing value, samurai debt, famines, and the shock of Western gunboats (1853).

outcome.value: Overthrown. Yoshinobu resigned (1867), and the Meiji Restoration (1868) and Boshin War ended shogunal rule.

sources.value: Shogunate and domain records, Dutch reports, and abundant printed sources. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Totman (1993).

overallCertainty.value: High for events. The start is dated 1600 (Sekigahara) or 1603 (Ieyasu becomes shogun). Population figures are estimates.
